title: Why Did Instagram Really Change Its Icon?
excerpt: The change has less to do with design trends than with Instagram's own positioning and its plans for the future.
body:
The change has less to do with design trends than with Instagram's own positioning and its plans for the future.

Three years ago Apple shipped iOS 7, and the "flat design" movement swept the internet along with it. After a brief argument, designers and creative directors lined up to spit on the corpse of skeuomorphism, shouting: "Down with gradients! Down with blurred backgrounds!"

Then, on May 13, perhaps the last giant app still holding on to a retro look (yes, five years ago already counts as the internet's last century) got a makeover too. Instagram's famous imitation Polaroid camera, colored glass lens and black viewfinder were replaced by a white icon on a rainbow background, and the interface dropped blue for black and white.

![Instagram's old and new icons](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607031222580bCGQZR3LwudiUKA.gif-w600Gif)

Leading the change was Instagram's new head of design, Ian Spalter, who had worked at YouTube and at R/GA, a creative agency for digital products, where he helped design the Nike+ app. He said he was braced for the anger: "I might need to take a vacation in a bunker." Cole Rise, who designed Instagram's previous icon, said after the new one went live: "Today's going to be fun."

The response was many times fiercer than "fun." The news item QDaily ran yesterday drew 150 comments, and more than half of them came down to the same thought: ugly, I refuse to update. Comments from users abroad ran the same way, only with more variety in the wording. Spalter published a long blog post and two videos explaining where the team's ideas came from and how it worked; the WeChat official account Wuyun Zhuangbanzhe translated the post and closed with: "I read the whole explanation and I still can't accept it, goodbye.gif."

"Honestly, praise or criticism, people telling brands what to do with their logos has become a more and more obvious trend. People enjoy sharing their opinions on social media, and that cuts both ways. The whole world has gotten more 'expert' than it used to be," Remy Jauffret, communication design lead at the innovation consultancy IDEO, told QDaily.

Instagram clearly made a high-risk decision. An app's icon alone takes up most of its visual identity, and Instagram has 400 million users worldwide, whose tastes could never line up. When people talk about how Instagram succeeded, the thing they mention most often is that it barely changed: it launched its first version in 2010 and announced more than 400 million active users at the end of 2015, and in between it never significantly reworked its interface or its features.

Until last August, for instance, every photo on Instagram was square — so much so that people now see any square photo on social media and think of Instagram. When the company shipped version 6.0 in 2014, the question it set out to answer was how to add a large number of photo-editing tools while keeping the interface clean instead of letting it swell.

![Instagram's interface across versions](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703122259jbhW1LtMPHFZwpzV.gif-w600Gif)

So here is the question. If the Instagram team had been cautious for so long, why ship an update in a completely different style all at once? Having held the line this long, why change now?

## Why do people think it has become "mediocre"?

One detail of the new icon: the little black square that stood for the viewfinder has been reduced to a white dot, and paired with the white circle that stands for the lens, it now suggests a smartphone camera and flash rather than a Polaroid lens and viewfinder. That is one of the large, quiet shifts photography has made in people's lives over the past decade.

This is the reality the "new humans" meet. People who grew up in the smartphone era may not be able to picture a Polaroid with a viewfinder, and they do not need a camera to teach them what taking a photo is. In today's context, the old design mostly stands for artiness and nostalgia — which is to say, for something of a niche.

"I don't think the Polaroid icon won people over because it was a great design in itself. It benefited from the commercial success of the product. Enormous numbers of users have poured so much of themselves into this app," Jauffret said.

Meanwhile, most apps now present a modern face (open the App Store and count how many camera apps still look like a camera). Instagram redesigning its app is barely news; the surprising part is that it took this long. Back then the Polaroid icon's skeuomorphism fit Apple's own design standards. But once Apple forced its system over to a flat style, keeping the old icon would have made Instagram look badly dated.

"Seen another way, this is already the result of Instagram taking users' feelings into account," said Huang Yi, a visual designer at the design and strategy consultancy frog. After iOS 7 came out, he watched the App Store every day for apps that had updated — WeChat, Evernote, VSCO — and found plenty of inspiration in them. "But Instagram never changed. What was going on? I waited a long time for today."

![The new Instagram interface](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/2016070312230071DjhLEBoZuWYqGl.gif-w600Gif)

![Flattened logos](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703122301RhwY6meg9dGr53qc.jpg-w600)

The risk of doing it is the verdict people commonly hand down now: mediocre. And it is worth noting that the new design has to hold its own not only against other photo apps but against a much wider field of entertainment products.

"The old icon's colors were conservative and neutral. Color made up only 10 to 20 percent of it. You can call the rainbow an inheritance, but once the proportion changes, it has changed," Sun Kewen, an interaction designer at Designaffairs, told QDaily. "The colors and shapes of the new icon look a lot like those popular entertainment apps. Purer hues, higher brightness, rounder forms, fuzzier edges — these all read as juvenile. When we design, those two color schemes are aimed at different users."

Sun thinks "the current design is awkward. It is less recognizable, and new users feel nothing when they see it." A commenter named Hong wrote: "I just dragged it — Instagram — next to Meitu Xiuxiu, so my home screen still has a consistent beauty to it. Smile."

The new interface, unlike the icon, won broad support. Huang Yi said: "I wouldn't read the colorful icon and the black-and-white interface as inconsistent. They make the same point. The color comes from the photos users post. The old interface had blue in it, and that was Instagram's own brand color. It meant nothing to users."

If Instagram is a store, the new interface is shelving you hardly notice; all the attention goes to users' photos. Where user photos are not involved — the sign-up screen for new users, say — it still shows moving color.

## What kind of product does Instagram want to be?

Hu Yueshen, another visual designer at frog, believes "the one thing Instagram does best is add a filter and share it." QDaily has made the same point in its year-in-review coverage: Instagram's daily active users passed 400 million, more than Twitter's, and it has still stayed remarkably simple. That is the company's greatest strength.

But the question now is whether Instagram still wants users to see it as nothing more than a photo product.

Instagram reported US$600 million in advertising revenue for 2015, and eMarketer expects that figure to pass Twitter's and Google's as soon as 2017. If you read us regularly, none of this will surprise you. On Instagram, restaurants that chase good looks, influencers and anything new with visual appeal all find it easier to stand out. It has hatched new business models, and it has shown large companies where young consumers' enthusiasm lies. The clearest change is that the fashion industry has moved its announcements and its conversations onto Instagram wholesale, from launch events to new products.

What drives this system at speed is no longer a tool. It is an enormous community.

Li Jie, a visual designer at Designaffairs, believes Instagram's early users included a set of amateur and professional photographers who used it to make work, and that set off a wave. "Users back then cared more about image quality and expression. There was a sense of taking photographs seriously."

Zhang Lei teaches brand design in the advertising department at Shanghai Normal University. He told us: "My age means I prefer the old icon, but cutting ties with the old-camera image early matters for Instagram."

![Instagram's new interface on a phone](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703122301RY9loFHVJmNAOtei.jpg-w600)

We have written about Meitu Xiuxiu before, in a piece called 《美图落幕，为什么免费工具做到全球最大也没成一个赚钱的生意》 ("The Curtain Falls on Meitu: Why the World's Biggest Free Tool Never Became a Money-Making Business"). Our argument was that even the most successful photo tool in the world sees its advantage shrink to almost nothing as phone cameras keep getting better. And with iPhone growth slowing, the competition has gotten a notch crueler for companies like Meitu.

The days when you could build a free tool, sweep up tens of millions of users and make money off them are gone. For Instagram, the "everyone is a photographer" positioning still matters, but to keep the company running it has to strengthen the community — and to the more than 200,000 advertisers under contract with it, the number of users in that community is the only measure that counts.

At the same time, as more and more photo-editing features get built, Instagram cannot go on being a "professional photography tool" without changing the structure of its interface. Bundling everything into one big app is one option; spinning off companion apps is another. Layout, Hyperlapse and Boomerang handle photo collage, time-lapse and short video respectively, and each connects seamlessly back to Instagram to publish, exactly as you see today. That spreads the tool functions thinner still.

BuzzFeed once published figures showing that among the ways teenagers share and post photos on their phones, Instagram was the favorite: 32 percent of respondents called it their most important social tool, up from 17 percent in 2013.

From the standpoint of its users, its industry or its own survival, Instagram has no reason not to seize the trend.

## Why are users beside themselves?

As of now, #changeitback, the hashtag about the redesign, has 4,692 posts on Instagram. The many options Instagram showed in its official video became the focus of the attack, with users hitting pause over and over to pick the one they liked: "Why didn't you use this one?"

"The new brand image isn't the one users knew, and an app you use every day has become part of the scenery of our lives," said Yang Hongxiang, deputy design director at the branding consultancy Labbrand. The new icon did not carry its visual assets forward properly, he said, which made it harder to recognize, so "our Instagram" seemed to vanish from the screen.

A large company usually changes its logo in one of two situations: a brand in its early stages wants to be recognized and to sharpen its personality, or a brand already leading its category wants to state a position and put its values across. Xu Jiajie, design director at DDB Shanghai, calls designing a logo a self-contradictory math problem: "It has to be beautiful, it has to be one of a kind, it has to carry a story, and people still have to understand it. Something has to go."

What gives internet companies their nerve is that apps are never afraid to iterate. Changing a mark the traditional way costs a great deal: once the mark changes, complicated printed materials have to be redone in full. Yang Hongxiang thinks Instagram, a dominant internet brand, faces far less risk in changing its. GAP withdrew its logo redesign years ago because the design had been chosen by public vote in a contest. A large company changed its mark without thinking it through from the market, the brand or the user; a contest alone decided the mark; the new logo could not carry the brand's core meaning and collided with what consumers thought GAP was. Pulling it was inevitable.

"When a brand or an organization outgrows its original business intent, or extends into different products, or when leadership wants to attract new customers, any of these can call for a new brand identity," Jauffret said. "Change always makes people uncomfortable, and then it dies down. I think time is the only test of truth."

So why mind? You will get used to it, and the thought "I'm deleting this" will barely cross your mind.

Doug Bowman, Google's former visual design lead, has a line people quote often: a logo redesign follows the famous 80/20 rule. At first 20 percent of people like it and 80 percent hate it; two years later the same 20 percent still like it, and the other 80 percent no longer care.
